title: Change what git shows you without changing history
summary: git replace substitutes one object for another at read time. Stitch a truncated history back onto its archive, correct a botched commit message locally, and see why the shas never change.
mental_model: Every command that reads an object checks `refs/replace/<sha>` first. If a replacement exists, git uses it instead — so history appears different while every original object, and every sha, stays exactly as it was.

setup.run: git commit -q -m "Iniital comit with a typo in the mesage"

steps.title: A commit message nobody can fix
steps.why: The typo is in the first commit, so amending it would rewrite every commit after it. On a shared repository that is a coordinated migration — for a spelling mistake.
steps.expect: The typo, and the root commit's sha which we will not be changing.

steps.title: Build a corrected copy of that commit
steps.why: `commit-tree` makes a new commit with the same tree and the same parents but a better message. It is an addition to the object database, not a modification — the original is untouched.

actions.run: sh -c 'root=$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD); git commit-tree $root^{tree} -m "Initial commit" > .git/fixed-root'

steps.expect: A new commit object with the corrected message, invisible to git log because nothing points at it.

verify.label: a corrected copy of the commit exists

steps.title: Substitute it
steps.why: `git replace <original> <replacement>` writes a ref under `refs/replace/`. Every read of the original sha now returns the replacement — so the log reads correctly while nothing was rewritten.
steps.expect: The typo is gone from the log, and a replace ref exists.

verify.label: the log no longer shows the typo

steps.title: Prove nothing was rewritten
steps.why: The other commits' shas are unchanged, because their parent pointers still name the original object. This is exactly what a rebase cannot do, and the entire reason `replace` exists.
steps.expect: The same shas either way — only the message shown differs.

verify.label: the original object is still there, unmodified

steps.title: The serious use: stitch a truncated history back on
steps.why: Repositories are often truncated to keep clones small, and the old history archived. `replace` can graft the archive back on for the afternoon you need to run blame across the join — then be removed again.

actions.run: sh -c 'git commit-tree $(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD)^{tree} -m "Historical archive root" > .git/archive-root'
sh -c 'root=$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD); git commit-tree $root^{tree} -p $(cat .git/archive-root) -m "Initial commit" > .git/grafted-root'

steps.expect: One extra commit appears at the root — history grew without any commit being rewritten.

verify.label: the grafted history is visible
verify.hint: replace the root with a copy that has the archive as its parent

verify.label: …while the real history is still three commits

steps.title: Replacements are local unless you push them
steps.why: `refs/replace/*` is an ordinary ref namespace, so it needs an explicit refspec like notes do. That is a feature: a graft that helps you today does not have to become everyone's problem.
steps.expect: Two replacement refs, both purely local.

steps.title: Remove them and check the repository is untouched
steps.why: Deleting the replace refs restores the original view instantly. Nothing has to be recovered, because nothing was ever changed — which is why this is the safest tool in the rewriting toolbox.
steps.expect: The typo is back, three commits, and a clean fsck. The replacement commits are still in the object database as dangling objects until gc runs — harmless, and proof nothing was ever destroyed.

verify.label: the original history is back, exactly as it always was
the repository is exactly as it started — replace never rewrites anything
the object database is healthy (--no-dangling: the replacement commits are now unreferenced, which is expected)
the archive mirror still holds the real history

pitfalls: Replacements are read-time only. A fetch, a push or a fresh clone sees the originals — anyone relying on a replacement without it being pushed sees different history from you.
`git replace` on a commit whose descendants you then rebase bakes the replacement in permanently, because the rebase reads through it. Remove replacements before rewriting.
`--no-replace-objects` is the escape hatch for debugging: it shows what is really there. Reach for it whenever git's output disagrees with another clone's.
The old `.git/info/grafts` file did something similar and is deprecated — it was silent, unshareable and easy to forget. `replace` is its supported successor.
Because replacements are invisible in normal output, document any you keep. A repository that shows different history to different people is a debugging nightmare.
cheatsheet: substitute one object for another at read time
share them, if you really mean to
